name: Pediatric anterior approach to the distal humerus
region: anterior pediatric elbow and distal arm
corridor: Anterior lazy-Z exposure along the appropriate border of biceps: medial for brachial artery and median nerve, lateral for radial nerve

positioning.text: Position supine with the arm on a radiolucent support and the antecubital region accessible to orthopedic and vascular teams.

setup.text: Document a structured preoperative motor, sensory, pulse, Doppler, temperature, color, and capillary-refill examination and confirm vascular expertise and repair capability.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the antecubital crease, biceps tendon, medial and lateral biceps borders, brachial pulse, and traumatic wound or skin-pucker site.

incision.text: Use a limited lazy-Z anterior incision for closed injury; incorporate and safely extend an existing open wound when present.

superficial_interval.text: Develop the interval beside biceps according to the target structure while protecting superficial veins and cutaneous nerves.

deep_interval.text: Work medial to biceps for brachial artery or median nerve and along the lateral biceps-brachioradialis border for radial nerve; do not divide the pediatric biceps tendon.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous antecubital tissue, biceps-border interval, disrupted brachialis/fascia, then fracture and neurovascular bundle.

structures_encountered.text: Biceps, brachialis, brachial artery, median nerve, radial nerve, brachioradialis, and displaced distal-humeral fragments may be encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Brachial artery, median/anterior interosseous nerve, radial nerve, superficial veins, and the biceps tendon are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Stabilize the fracture before definitive vessel or nerve repair and reassess perfusion after reduction; a persistently pale, cool, poorly perfused hand requires urgent exploration.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract biceps rather than dividing its tendon and avoid traction or clamp injury to an entrapped or contused neurovascular structure.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to brachial artery and median nerve medially or radial nerve laterally after severe supracondylar displacement.

limitations.text: This is a targeted neurovascular exploration rather than the routine exposure for supracondylar fracture fixation.

extensions.text: Extend the lateral interval distally toward radial-nerve division or extend the medial interval only enough for safe vascular control and repair.

indications.text: Indications include persistent dysvascularity after reduction/fixation and selected open injuries or new post-reduction nerve deficits with suspected entrapment.

relative_contraindications.text: A well-perfused pulseless hand or isolated initial neurapraxia is not by itself an automatic indication for exploration; management requires serial examination and individualized judgment.

implant_implications.text: Reassess the hand after provisional reduction and each wire; remove and redirect any wire temporally associated with new ischemia or nerve dysfunction.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Maintain imaging access for reduction and stable pin fixation before definitive vascular or nerve repair.

closure.text: Confirm flow and nerve continuity without compression, then close loosely with fine absorbable pediatric sutures and continue documented serial neurovascular checks.

complications.text: Complications include persistent ischemia, thrombosis, compartment syndrome, Volkmann contracture, median/radial neuropathy, stiffness, infection, and iatrogenic vessel injury.

bailouts.text: If primary arterial repair is not possible, obtain proximal/distal control and proceed with vascular reconstruction rather than accepting inadequate perfusion.

procedure_applications.condition: A persistently dysvascular limb or defined nerve-entrapment concern requires direct exploration after reduction and stabilization

questions.question: Which biceps border exposes the brachial artery?
Which finding most clearly mandates exploration?
questions.answer: Persistent poor perfusion with a pale, cool, pulseless hand after reduction and fixation.

questions.question: Should the pediatric biceps tendon be divided?
